western-chagatai-khanate.t: The Transoxianan half of the divided Chagatai Khanate, ruled in practice by Turkic amirs and the springboard for Timur's rise.
western-chagatai-khanate.o: The Chagatai Khanate split in the 1340s. In the west, the Qara'unas amir Qazaghan defeated and killed Khan Qazan in 1346 or 1347, after which Transoxiana was governed by amirs who set up puppet khans of Chagatai or Ögedei descent, while the east became Moghulistan.
western-chagatai-khanate.r: Real power lay with the Turkic and Mongol tribal amirs of the Barlas, Jalayir, Arlat and Qara'unas, who had settled among the towns of Transoxiana and adopted Islam. Qazaghan ruled as amir until his murder in 1358, after which rival amirs fought for control. The region was invaded twice by Tughlugh Timur of Moghulistan, in 1360 and 1361.
western-chagatai-khanate.e: Out of these struggles rose Timur of the Barlas, first allied with and then against Amir Husayn, Qazaghan's grandson. In 1370 Timur defeated Husayn at Balkh and took power, ruling through a puppet Chagatai khan and founding the Timurid Empire.

west-francia.t: Western third of the Carolingian realm, created at Verdun in 843, out of which the Kingdom of France grew.
west-francia.o: After civil war among the sons of Louis the Pious, the Treaty of Verdun in 843 gave Charles the Bald the lands west of the Scheldt, Meuse, Saône and Rhône. His realm took in Neustria, Aquitaine, Gascony and the Spanish March, though Brittany remained largely independent.
west-francia.r: Royal power weakened under the pressure of Viking raids and of great regional magnates who turned their offices into hereditary principalities. Charles the Bald ordered fortified bridges in the Edict of Pîtres in 864. Count Odo of Paris defended the city against the Vikings in 885 to 886 and was elected king, beginning a rivalry between Carolingians and his Robertian family.
west-francia.e: In 911 Charles the Simple granted Rollo the land that became the Duchy of Normandy. Kings alternated between the two families until the last Carolingian, Louis V, died in 987, when the magnates elected Hugh Capet, founding the Kingdom of France.

wari-empire.t: The first expansionist state of the Andean highlands, which built a network of administrative centres and roads across Peru centuries before the Incas.
wari-empire.o: Wari arose around 600 CE in the Ayacucho basin of the central Peruvian highlands, drawing on the local Huarpa culture and religious imagery shared with Tiwanaku. Its capital, Wari, grew into a city of perhaps 40,000 people covering several square kilometres.
wari-empire.r: From its capital Wari established planned provincial centres such as Pikillacta near Cusco, Viracochapampa in the north and Cerro Baúl in Moquegua, facing Tiwanaku. These rectangular compounds suggest a centralised administration that controlled labour and goods. Wari built terraces and roads that the Incas later reused, and may have used early khipus for records. Its tapestry tunics and colourful pottery spread a common style. Tombs at El Castillo de Huarmey show the wealth of Wari noblewomen.
wari-empire.e: The Wari state broke up around 1000, perhaps owing to drought and internal conflict, and its centres were abandoned. Its administrative model and roads influenced later states, notably the Inca Empire, while regional powers such as the Chanka Confederation and the Kingdom of Chimor rose in its wake.

western-wei-206-bc.t: Wei Bao's kingdom in southern Shanxi, one of the Eighteen Kingdoms of 206 BCE, conquered by Han Xin's surprise crossing of the Yellow River.
western-wei-206-bc.o: Wei Bao, of the royal house of the old State of Wei, had been made King of Wei during the rising against the Qin dynasty. In Xiang Yu's settlement of 206 BCE he lost the Wei heartland around Daliang and was moved west to rule as King of Western Wei from Pingyang in the Fen valley of Shanxi.
western-wei-206-bc.r: The kingdom covered the Hedong region, rich in salt and grain, on the east bank of the Yellow River facing the Guanzhong region. It was a frontline state whose loyalty swung with the fortunes of Chu and Han.
western-wei-206-bc.e: Wei Bao joined Liu Bang in 205 BCE, then deserted him after the Han defeat at Pengcheng. That autumn Han Xin feinted at one ford while crossing at Xiayang on rafts of wooden jars, and captured Wei Bao. His concubine Bo Ji later bore Liu Bang a son, the future Emperor Wen of Han.

wusun.t: Nomads of the Ili valley and Issyk-Kul who became the Han dynasty's chief steppe ally against the Xiongnu, sealed by marriages to Chinese princesses.
wusun.o: The Wusun first lived near the Yuezhi in the Gansu region and were subject to the Xiongnu. Their ruler, the kunmo Liejiaomi, raised by the Xiongnu, led them west around 161 BCE to the Ili valley and the Issyk-Kul basin, driving out the Yuezhi and the Saka who had settled there.
wusun.r: The Han envoy Zhang Qian visited around 115 BCE seeking an alliance. The Wusun were pastoralists with large horse herds and, by Han count, some 630,000 people, ruled by the kunmo from the Red Valley city of Chigu. Han princesses, including Liu Xijun, who wrote a famous lament on her exile, married Wusun rulers, and in 71 BCE a joint Han-Wusun campaign struck the Xiongnu. A dual kingship of greater and lesser kunmo developed after 53 BCE.
wusun.e: The Wusun weakened through internal division and pressure from the Rouran Khaganate, moving into the Pamirs in the 5th century, after which they disappear as a distinct power. Their remnants merged into later Turkic peoples of the Zhetysu region.

wild-and-rhinegraviate.t: A county on the Nahe and in the Hunsrück whose Wild- and Rhinegraves, ancestors of the princes of Salm, ruled from castles above Kirn.
wild-and-rhinegraviate.o: The Wildgraves held lands in the Hunsrück and on the Nahe, while the Rhinegraves ruled around Rheingrafenstein. In 1409 the Rhinegrave John III inherited the Wildgraviate, uniting both titles as Wild- and Rhinegraves. A marriage in 1475 later brought them half of the county of Salm in the Vosges.
wild-and-rhinegraviate.r: The family repeatedly divided its lands into branches such as Dhaun, Kyrburg and Grumbach, with Kyrburg castle above Kirn as a main seat. Most branches became Lutheran, though some Salm lines returned to Catholicism. The counts often served as officers in French and imperial armies, and branches were raised to princes as Salm-Salm and Salm-Kyrburg in the 17th and 18th centuries.
wild-and-rhinegraviate.e: French revolutionary armies occupied the left bank of the Rhine in 1794, ending the family's rule there. Compensated in 1803 with secularised lands in Westphalia, the princes of Salm formed the Principality of Salm, which France annexed in 1811.

wuyue.t: A peaceful and prosperous coastal kingdom around Hangzhou, famous for its Buddhist pagodas and sea trade, that handed itself over to the Song without a fight.
wuyue.o: Qian Liu, a former salt smuggler who became a soldier, defeated the rebel Dong Chang in 896 and gained control of the Zhejiang coast. In 907 the Later Liang named him Prince of Wuyue, and he governed from Qiantang (modern Hangzhou).
wuyue.r: The Qian rulers generally accepted the suzerainty of the northern dynasties, avoiding major wars except with their neighbour Wu (Ten Kingdoms) and its successor Southern Tang. They built sea walls along the Qiantang river, drained and irrigated land, and traded by sea with the Khitan, Korea and Japan. Wuyue was a great centre of Buddhism, and the Leifeng and Baochu pagodas of Hangzhou date from its rule.
wuyue.e: Qian Chu, the last king, helped the Song Dynasty conquer Southern Tang and in 978 surrendered his whole kingdom to Song without bloodshed. The Qian family was honoured at the Song court, and Hangzhou later became the Southern Song capital.

western-chu.t: The kingdom of Xiang Yu, Hegemon-King of Western Chu, who destroyed the Qin armies and redrew China's map, only to lose it all to Liu Bang at Gaixia in 202 BCE.
western-chu.o: Xiang Yu, grandson of the Chu general Xiang Yan, rose with his uncle Xiang Liang in the rebellion against the Qin dynasty. After his victory at Julu in 207 BCE he took Xianyang, killed the surrendered Qin ruler Ziying and burned the palaces. In 206 BCE he divided the empire into eighteen kingdoms and took for himself the title of Hegemon-King of Western Chu, ruling from Pengcheng (Xuzhou).
western-chu.r: Western Chu held nine commanderies of the old State of Chu and the State of Wei. Xiang Yu dominated the other kings by military force, but he alienated allies, had his nominal sovereign Emperor Yi of Chu killed in 205 BCE and treated defeated enemies brutally. His crushing victory over Liu Bang at Pengcheng was never turned into lasting advantage.
western-chu.e: Over four years of Chu-Han war, Liu Bang's alliances wore Western Chu down. Surrounded at Gaixia in 202 BCE and hearing Chu songs from the enemy camp, Xiang Yu broke out and killed himself by the Wu River. Liu Bang then founded the Han Dynasty.

wu-ten-kingdoms.t: The first of the southern Ten Kingdoms, ruled from Yangzhou by the Yang family and their powerful ministers, which became the basis of Southern Tang.
wu-ten-kingdoms.o: Yang Xingmi, a soldier of humble origins, won control of the Huainan region between the Huai and Yangtze rivers in the 890s and made Yangzhou his base. The Tang named him Prince of Wu in 902, and after the dynasty fell in 907 his family refused to recognise the Later Liang.
wu-ten-kingdoms.r: Wu was rich from salt production and Yangtze trade, and fought repeated wars with Wuyue and the northern dynasties. Yang Xingmi's sons were weak, and real power passed to the general Xu Wen and his adopted son Xu Zhigao, who ran the government from Jinling (Nanjing). Yang Pu took the title of emperor in 927.
wu-ten-kingdoms.e: In 937 Xu Zhigao made Yang Pu abdicate and founded his own dynasty, soon renamed Tang and known as Southern Tang, taking the name Li Bian. The Yang family was kept in confinement and later massacred.

wu-zhou.t: The Zhou dynasty proclaimed by Wu Zetian, the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor in her own name, interrupting the Tang from 690 to 705.
wu-zhou.o: Wu Zhao, a concubine of Emperor Taizong, became empress to Emperor Gaozong in 655 and gradually took over government as he fell ill. After his death in 683 she deposed her son Zhongzong, kept Ruizong as a figurehead, crushed a Tang princes' revolt and in 690 proclaimed her own Zhou dynasty, with Luoyang, renamed Shendu, as capital.
wu-zhou.r: Wu Zetian promoted Buddhism, using the Great Cloud Sutra to support a female ruler, and favoured the Maitreya cult. She widened the examination system to recruit men from outside the old north-western aristocracy, invented new written characters and relied on informers and secret police such as Lai Junchen. The frontier wars against the Second Turkic Khaganate, Khitan and Tibetans had mixed results.
wu-zhou.e: In 705 ministers led by Zhang Jianzhi killed her favourites, the Zhang brothers, and forced the aged Wu Zetian to abdicate in favour of Zhongzong, restoring the Tang Dynasty. She died later that year and was buried with Gaozong at the Qianling mausoleum.

wambu-kingdom.t: An Ovimbundu kingdom of the central Angolan highlands whose lands became the site of the colonial city of Huambo.
wambu-kingdom.o: Wambu (Huambo) was one of the Ovimbundu kingdoms that emerged on the Benguela highlands by the 18th century, alongside the Bailundo Kingdom and the Viye Kingdom. Like its neighbours, it grew as a fortified raiding state with ruling lineages of mixed local and immigrant origin.
wambu-kingdom.r: Its kings ruled from hilltop fortresses through titled officials and village heads. Wambu's people farmed maize and beans and joined Ovimbundu long-distance caravans carrying slaves, ivory, beeswax and later rubber between the interior and Benguela. Detailed records of its rulers are scarce.
wambu-kingdom.e: Wambu was drawn into the Bailundo revolt of 1902 and occupied by Portuguese forces by 1902–03. In 1912 the Portuguese founded the city of Huambo on its lands, which became one of Angola's main cities.

wattasid-sultanate.t: The family of Marinid viziers who became sultans of Fez, ruling a shrunken Morocco squeezed between Portuguese enclaves and the rising Saadis.
wattasid-sultanate.o: The Banu Wattas, Zenata kin of the Marinids, governed Morocco as regents and viziers from 1420. After the last Marinid sultan was killed in Fez in 1465, a sharif ruled the city until Muhammad al-Shaykh al-Wattasi, who had just lost Arzila to Portugal in 1471, captured Fez in 1472 and proclaimed himself sultan.
wattasid-sultanate.r: Wattasid authority rarely reached far beyond Fez and the north. The Hintata emirate held Marrakesh, local lords ruled Chefchaouen and Tetouan, and the Kingdom of Portugal seized much of the Atlantic coast. The dynasty relied on truces with Portugal and the prestige of Fez's scholars, while Sufi brotherhoods led resistance to the Christians.
wattasid-sultanate.e: The Saadi Sultanate, leading holy war from the south, defeated the Wattasids and took Fez in 1549. Ali Abu Hassun briefly retook the city in 1554 with Ottoman help from the Regency of Algiers, but was killed the same year, ending the dynasty.

wuhuan.t: Nomads of the north-eastern frontier who served the Han as border guards and cavalry until Cao Cao crushed them at White Wolf Mountain in 207.
wuhuan.o: Like the Xianbei, the Wuhuan were survivors of the Donghu, who took refuge at the Wuhuan mountains after Modu of the Xiongnu destroyed them around 206 BCE. They lived in eastern Inner Mongolia and western Liaoning and paid tribute to the Xiongnu.
wuhuan.r: After the Han general Huo Qubing defeated the Xiongnu in 119 BCE, the Han Dynasty resettled Wuhuan bands along its frontier commanderies as guards and set up a Protector of the Wuhuan. They were herders and hunters ruled by elected chiefs, without a single king, and Wuhuan cavalry became famous mercenaries in Han wars.
wuhuan.e: In the late 2nd century Wuhuan chiefs such as Tadun allied with the warlord Yuan Shao. In 207 Cao Cao crossed the mountains and killed Tadun at White Wolf Mountain, then moved the Wuhuan into China, where their horsemen served his armies and they gradually merged with the Chinese and the Xianbei.

western-zhou.t: The dynasty that overthrew the Shang, introduced the idea of the Mandate of Heaven and ruled northern China through kinsmen planted across the land.
western-zhou.o: The Zhou were a people of the Wei River valley in Shaanxi who grew strong under King Wen. His son King Wu defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at Muye in 1046 BCE. After Wu's early death the Duke of Zhou acted as regent for the young King Cheng, crushed a rebellion of Shang loyalists and royal brothers, and built an eastern capital at Luoyi.
western-zhou.r: The kings ruled from Haojing and Fengjing near modern Xi'an and justified their power as the Mandate of Heaven, given to virtuous rulers and withdrawn from wicked ones. They granted lands to relatives and allies, who founded states such as the State of Lu, the State of Jin and the State of Yan. Long bronze inscriptions record appointments, gifts and lawsuits. In 841 BCE nobles expelled King Li, the first exactly dated year in Chinese history.
western-zhou.e: In 771 BCE the Marquis of Shen and the Quanrong sacked Haojing and killed King You. King Ping re-established the court at Luoyang, beginning the Eastern Zhou. Later Confucians idealised the early Western Zhou as China's golden age of ritual order.
western-zhou.re: Zhou ancestral religion and worship of Heaven

western-xia.t: The empire of the Tangut people in north-west China, with its own script and Buddhist culture, destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1227.
western-xia.o: The Tanguts were a Tibeto-Burman people whose Tuoba chiefs governed the Xiazhou region in the Ordos as Tang and Song governors. Li Jiqian broke with the Song in 982, his son Li Deming expanded west into the Hexi Corridor, and in 1038 Li Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor of Great Xia, with his capital at Xingqing (modern Yinchuan).
western-xia.r: Western Xia combined a tribal military aristocracy with Chinese-style ministries. Li Yuanhao introduced a distinctive Tangut script in 1036, used for laws, histories and a huge translation of the Buddhist canon. The state controlled trade routes between China and Central Asia and fought the Song Dynasty, the Liao dynasty and the Jin dynasty (1115-1234), extracting subsidies from Song after 1044.
western-xia.e: The Mongols attacked from 1205. After Western Xia refused to join the campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire, Genghis Khan invaded in 1226; he died during the siege in 1227, and the capital fell soon after. The Tangut population was massacred or scattered.

witbooi-nama.t: The Nama community of Gibeon led by Hendrik Witbooi, the most persistent opponent of German colonial rule in Namibia.
witbooi-nama.o: The Witboois, or Khowesin, were an Oorlam group from the northern Cape. Around 1863 Kido Witbooi led them north from Pella to Gibeon in central southern Namibia, where a Rhenish mission was established and they became one of the leading Nama communities.
witbooi-nama.r: Hendrik Witbooi, grandson of Kido, saw himself as a Christian leader with a divine mission and fought long campaigns against the Herero for cattle and land. Literate and politically shrewd, he kept letters and a diary that are major sources. He refused German protection until a surprise German attack on his base at Hornkranz in 1893 forced him to submit in 1894.
witbooi-nama.e: Witbooi fought as a German ally for ten years, then rose against German South West Africa in October 1904. He was killed in 1905, and the Witbooi were deported, many dying on Shark Island; his image appears on Namibian banknotes.

west-ukrainian-peoples-republic.t: The Ukrainian state of eastern Galicia, proclaimed in Lviv in 1918, which fought Poland and briefly united with the Ukrainian People's Republic.
west-ukrainian-peoples-republic.o: As the Austro-Hungarian Empire collapsed, Ukrainian soldiers seized Lviv on 1 November 1918, and a Ukrainian National Council proclaimed the West Ukrainian People's Republic over eastern Galicia, northern Bukovina and Transcarpathia. Yevhen Petrushevych became its president and Kost Levytsky headed the government.
west-ukrainian-peoples-republic.r: The republic quickly built a working administration, police and courts out of former Austrian institutions and formed the disciplined Ukrainian Galician Army. Polish residents of Lviv resisted, and the Polish-Ukrainian War began; the Ukrainians lost Lviv in November and moved the capital to Ternopil and then Stanislaviv. In January 1919 the republic proclaimed union with the Ukrainian People's Republic, keeping its own government.
west-ukrainian-peoples-republic.e: A Polish offensive in mid 1919 drove the Galician Army across the Zbruch in July, and the Second Polish Republic occupied the whole territory. Petrushevych's government went into exile, and the Allies recognised Polish rule over eastern Galicia in 1923.

western-kara-khanid-khanate.t: The western branch of the Kara-Khanid dynasty, ruling Samarkand and Bukhara under Seljuk and then Qara Khitai overlordship.
western-kara-khanid-khanate.o: When the Kara-Khanid Khanate divided around 1042, the descendants of Ibrahim Tamghach Khan's line took Transoxiana, with Samarkand as their capital. Ibrahim Tamghach Khan himself was the founding ruler, establishing a strong, centralised state.
western-kara-khanid-khanate.r: Ibrahim Tamghach Khan was remembered for justice, founding hospitals and madrasas in Samarkand. The khans ruled a settled Persian-speaking population with Turkic troops, and Bukhara was governed in time by the hereditary Burhan family of religious leaders. In 1089 the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah took Samarkand, making the khans vassals.
western-kara-khanid-khanate.e: After the Qara Khitai crushed the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar at the Qatwan steppe in 1141, the khans became Qara Khitai vassals. The last khan, Uthman, was executed in 1212 by Muhammad II of the Khwarazmian Empire after a revolt in Samarkand.

wahidi-sultanate.t: A coastal sultanate of the Wahidi tribe, centred on Balhaf, near the site of the ancient incense port of Qana.
wahidi-sultanate.o: The Wahidi tribe held the coast and hinterland between the Aulaqi lands and Hadramawt. The territory was divided among several branches, and the sultanate based at Balhaf emerged as a separate ruling line by around 1830.
wahidi-sultanate.r: The sultans ruled a coastal strip and valleys inland, living from fishing, farming and trade. Near Bir Ali in their territory lay the ruins of Qana, the main port of the ancient Kingdom of Hadramawt. The Wahidi sultanates signed treaties with Britain in the late 19th century and formed part of the Aden Protectorate. Balhaf joined the Federation of South Arabia in the early 1960s.
wahidi-sultanate.e: In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over the region and the sultanate was abolished and incorporated into South Yemen.

warmians.t: Prussian people of Warmia, around the Vistula Lagoon, whose land became the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia after the Teutonic conquest.
warmians.o: The Warmians lived in Warmia, south-east of the Vistula Lagoon in today's northern Poland. They were one of the Prussian peoples recorded by Peter of Dusburg, with settlements along the Pasłęka and Łyna rivers.
warmians.r: Warmian society was led by nobles who held hillforts and controlled farming land, and its people kept the Prussian religion. The coast linked them to Baltic trade, including amber.
warmians.e: The Teutonic Order invaded in 1239, founding Balga castle, and soon dominated Warmia. During the Great Prussian Uprising the Warmians fought under their leader Glappe, who was captured and hanged at Königsberg. By 1274 they were subdued, and their land became the Bishopric of Warmia, a prince-bishopric that passed to Poland in 1466.

western-turkic-khaganate.t: The western half of the Turkic empire, which ruled the steppe from the Altai to the Volga and the oasis cities of Sogdiana and the Tarim.
western-turkic-khaganate.o: The First Turkic Khaganate, founded in 552 by Bumin, gave its western lands to his brother Istämi, who with Persia destroyed the Hephthalite Empire. Rivalries within the ruling Ashina clan led to a formal split around 603, when Tardu's successors ruled the west independently of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate.
western-turkic-khaganate.r: The khagans ruled from summer pastures and courts such as Suyab in the Chu valley over the 'On Oq', ten arrows or tribes in two wings. Sogdian merchants and scribes served them, and they sent embassies to Byzantium, allying with Heraclius against Persia in 627. Under Tong Yabghu, whom Xuanzang met in 630, the khaganate reached its height, collecting tribute from Sogdian cities and Tokharistan.
western-turkic-khaganate.e: After Tong Yabghu's murder, civil wars divided the tribes, and in 657 the Tang general Su Dingfang defeated the khagan Ashina Helu. The Ashina were installed as Tang puppets until about 742; power passed to the Turgesh Khaganate and the Karluk Yabgu.

weimar-republic.t: Germany's first parliamentary democracy, born of defeat in 1918 and destroyed by depression and the rise of the Nazis.
weimar-republic.o: The German Empire collapsed in November 1918 with naval mutinies and revolution. On 9 November Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a republic in Berlin as William II abdicated. A national assembly met in Weimar to avoid unrest in the capital and adopted a democratic constitution in August 1919, with Friedrich Ebert as president.
weimar-republic.r: The republic faced the Treaty of Versailles, the Kapp Putsch, political murders and the hyperinflation of 1923, when the French occupied the Ruhr. Under Gustav Stresemann it stabilised, joined the League of Nations and saw a cultural flowering in Berlin, from the Bauhaus to cinema. The Great Depression brought mass unemployment and rule by emergency decree from 1930.
weimar-republic.e: President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Reichstag fire decree and the Enabling Act of March 1933 destroyed parliamentary rule, ending the republic and beginning Nazi Germany.

western-guo.t: A Ji-clan state that moved from the Wei valley to the Yellow River, leaving the rich Guo cemetery at Sanmenxia, and fell to Jin in the famous ruse of the borrowed road.
western-guo.o: Western Guo was founded by a brother of King Wen of Zhou near Baoji in the Wei River valley. Around the end of the Western Zhou, its rulers moved east to Shangyang, near modern Sanmenxia in Henan, controlling a key crossing on the Yellow River.
western-guo.r: The dukes of Guo were senior ministers at the Zhou court and led royal campaigns into the 7th century BCE. The Shangcunling cemetery at Sanmenxia, with chariot pits and the tomb of Guo Ji containing jade burial garments and one of China's earliest iron-bladed swords, shows the state's wealth.
western-guo.e: In 655 BCE Duke Xian of Jin, having bribed the State of Yu to let his army pass, captured Shangyang and ended Guo, then destroyed Yu on the way home. The episode gave Chinese the idiom 'borrowing a road to destroy Guo'.

white-horde.t: The eastern wing of the Golden Horde, ruled by descendants of Jochi's son Orda on the steppes of Kazakhstan.
white-horde.o: After Jochi, Genghis Khan's eldest son, died in 1227, his lands were divided. His eldest son Orda received the eastern part, the left wing of the ulus, east of the Ural River, with its own line of khans subordinate to the Golden Horde. Names of the 'White' and 'Blue' wings are used inconsistently in the sources.
white-horde.r: The khans of the Orda line ruled nomadic Turkic and Mongol tribes in the steppes of the Syr Darya and the Irtysh, with towns such as Sighnaq and Sauran on the Syr Darya. The Orda khans enjoyed considerable autonomy and sent their own envoys to the Yuan and Ilkhanid courts.
white-horde.e: In the late 14th century the White Horde khan Tokhtamysh, backed by Timur, reunited it with the Golden Horde in 1378. After further civil wars the eastern lands passed to Shibanid and other Jochid princes, notably Abu'l-Khayr of the Uzbek Khanate in 1428.

white-croats.t: A shadowy Slavic people north of the Carpathians, named by a Byzantine emperor as the homeland of the Croats of the Adriatic.
white-croats.o: The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII wrote in the 10th century of a White or unbaptised Croatia beyond Hungary, from which some Croats had migrated to Dalmatia in the 7th century. Historians usually place the White Croats on the upper Dniester and Vistula, on both slopes of the Carpathians, but their exact territory is disputed.
white-croats.r: Very little is known of their society. They appear to have lived in fortified hill settlements, such as the large site at Stilsko near Lviv, and to have farmed and herded in the Carpathian foothills. The Primary Chronicle lists Croats among the East Slavic tribes who took part in Oleg's campaign against Constantinople in 907.
white-croats.e: In 992 Vladimir I of Kievan Rus' campaigned against the Croats, and they disappear from the sources soon afterwards. Their eastern lands became part of Rus' and later the Principality of Galicia, while the western parts around Krakow passed to the Duchy of Poland.

wilusa.t: Wilusa, a kingdom of north-western Anatolia in Hittite texts, widely identified with Homer's Troy and its city of Ilios.
wilusa.o: Wilusa appears in Hittite records from the 15th century BCE, first as part of the Assuwa league. Most scholars identify it with Troy at Hisarlik, guarding the entrance to the Dardanelles, whose sixth and seventh cities were large walled citadels with a lower town.
wilusa.r: Its kings ruled as vassals of the Hittite Empire. Around 1280 BCE Muwatalli II made a treaty with Alaksandu of Wilusa, whose name resembles Alexandros, Homer's Paris, and the treaty invokes a god Appaliuna. Later letters show the Mycenaean king of Ahhiyawa contesting control of Wilusa and the deposition of a king named Walmu.
wilusa.e: Troy VIIa was destroyed by fire around 1180 BCE, at the end of the Late Bronze Age, and Wilusa vanishes from written sources. Greek epic transformed its memory into the story of the Trojan War.

western-liang-555-587.t: A small client state around Jiangling on the middle Yangtze, where a branch of the Liang imperial family reigned under Western Wei, Northern Zhou and Sui protection.
western-liang-555-587.o: In 554 Western Wei armies captured Jiangling and killed Emperor Yuan of Liang. The following year they installed his nephew Xiao Cha, a grandson of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and a rival of the Jiangling court, as emperor of a rump Liang state confined to the district around the city.
western-liang-555-587.r: Its emperors kept the full ceremony of a Chinese court, with reign titles and officials, but a Western Wei and later Northern Zhou garrison stood in Jiangling, and the rulers depended entirely on their northern patrons. The territory was only a few prefectures wide. Xiao Kui, the second emperor, was a respected scholar, and his daughter married Yang Guang, the future Emperor Yang of the Sui Dynasty.
western-liang-555-587.e: In 587 Emperor Wen of Sui summoned the third ruler, Xiao Cong, to Chang'an and abolished the state; some of its officials fled to the Chen dynasty. The Xiao family remained prominent under Sui and Tang thanks to the marriage tie.

willoughbyland.t: An English sugar colony on the Suriname river, founded from Barbados, that was lost to the Dutch in 1667 in exchange for New York.
willoughbyland.o: In 1650 Francis, Lord Willoughby of Parham, the royalist governor of Barbados, sent Anthony Rowse with settlers to the Suriname river in Guiana. In 1652 Willoughby visited the colony, and in 1662 he received a royal grant from Charles II. The capital was Torarica, a small town on the river.
willoughbyland.r: Willoughbyland grew quickly to several thousand people, with some fifty sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Sephardic Jewish settlers, some from Dutch Brazil, were granted privileges and founded settlements along the river that later became Jodensavanne. The writer Aphra Behn claimed to have lived there and set her novel Oroonoko in the colony. A governor ruled with an assembly of planters.
willoughbyland.e: In 1667, during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, a Zeeland fleet under Abraham Crijnssen captured the colony. The Treaty of Breda that year confirmed Dutch possession of Suriname in exchange for England keeping New Netherland, renamed New York. Many English planters left by 1680.

west-breifne.t: The O'Rourke lordship of Leitrim, heir to the old kingdom of Breifne, which lasted until the Elizabethan and Jacobean conquest.
west-breifne.o: When the Kingdom of Breifne split in 1256, the O'Rourkes held the western part, roughly modern County Leitrim, while the O'Reillys took the east. Dromahair, by Lough Gill, became the O'Rourke seat.
west-breifne.r: West Breifne was a land of small lakes, hills and cattle-raising, ruled through Gaelic law with bardic and learned families. The O'Rourkes founded Creevelea Friary in 1508. Brian O'Rourke sheltered Spanish Armada survivors in 1588 and was executed at Tyburn in 1591 for treason.
west-breifne.e: His son Brian Og fought with O'Neill in the Nine Years' War. After defeat the lordship was shired as County Leitrim and, in the early 17th century, planted with English settlers within the Kingdom of Ireland.
